```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r fits, include = FALSE}
data(srs)
data(classroom_wb)
items <- paste0("wb", 1:6)
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
cfit <- bm_cached("cwb_respondent")
```

Eight figures. Each answers one question, each returns a `ggplot`, and each can
be overridden with anything ggplot2 offers.

## The gallery

### 1. Where does the scale sit?

```{r p1, fig.alt = "Scale coefficient shown as a point with its confidence interval against the conventional landmarks at 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5."}
p_scale <- bm_plot_scale_h(fit)
p_scale
```

The landmarks are drawn as reference lines. They are conventions of the
tradition, not thresholds the software applies.

> **Minimum interpretation contract.** The interval is a repeated-sampling CI
> for a fixed declared item set. Its calibration applies to the scale
> coefficient only; item and pair intervals are uncalibrated. The landmark
> lines are descriptive guides, not tests.

### 2. What are the item-level H values in the declared scale?

```{r p2, fig.alt = "Item coefficients for the eleven SRS items, sorted in ascending order, each shown as a point on a common axis."}
bm_plot_item_h(fit, sort = TRUE)
```

Add `show_interval = TRUE` for item-level endpoints — uncorrected, and labelled
as such.

### 3. What are the pair-level H values in the declared scale?

```{r p3, fig.alt = "Lower-triangular heatmap of pair coefficients for the eleven items, with darker cells indicating higher pair scalability."}
bm_plot_pair_h(fit)
```

A triangle, not a square: each unordered pair appears once. Use
`layout = "scatter"` when the item count makes cells too small to read.

> **Inspection, not selection.** These two figures describe the fixed item set
> already declared in the fit. They do not select items or justify carrying the
> old scale interval to a reduced set. Dropping an item and refitting creates a
> new estimand and a new analysis.

### 4. Where did the interval come from?

```{r p4, fig.alt = "Bootstrap distribution of the scale coefficient with uncorrected and corrected endpoints marked beneath it."}
bm_plot_draws(fit)
```

### 5. Are there enough draws?

```{r p5, fig.alt = "Interval endpoints plotted against cumulative draw count, both flattening as draws accumulate."}
bm_plot_mc_stability(fit)
```

### 6. What does the correction do?

```{r p6, fig.alt = "Width multiplier for the binary correction plotted against sample size, falling toward one as the sample grows."}
bm_plot_calibration(mode = "binary")
```

This one runs with no data at all, which makes it useful for explaining the
method before an analysis exists.

### 7. How are the items distributed?

```{r p7, fig.alt = "Proportion endorsing each of the eleven SRS items, plotted as points on a common axis."}
bm_plot_margins(fit)
```

### 8. What do the clusters look like?

```{r p8, fig.alt = "Classrooms ordered by size showing the weight each population target assigns, with respondent weighting rising with size and equal-cluster weighting flat."}
bm_plot_clusters(classroom_wb$class_id, show_targets = TRUE)
```

## Customising

Every figure is a plain `ggplot` object, so nothing is closed to you:

```{r custom, fig.alt = "The item coefficient figure with a different theme, custom axis labels and a title applied on top of the package default."}
bm_plot_item_h(fit, sort = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Scientific Reasoning Scale",
       subtitle = "Item scalability, ascending") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Layer order is the usual ggplot2 rule: what you add last wins.

### The house theme on your own figures

```{r theme, fig.alt = "A line-and-point plot of a random walk drawn with the package theme applied, showing its typography and grid treatment."}
set.seed(42)
ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:20, y = cumsum(rnorm(20))), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "theme_bayesmokken() on an unrelated figure",
       x = "index", y = "value") +
  theme_bayesmokken()
```

```{r seed-note, include = FALSE}
# The chunk above is stochastic; the vignette-wide seed in _setup.R fixes it.
```

### Colours

```{r palette}
bm_palette(4)
```

```{r scales, fig.alt = "Four groups of points drawn in the package categorical palette, distinguished by both colour and plotting symbol."}
set.seed(43)
d <- data.frame(x = rep(1:10, 4), y = rnorm(40) + rep(1:4, each = 10),
                g = factor(rep(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), each = 10)))
ggplot(d, aes(x, y, colour = g, shape = g)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_bayesmokken() +
  theme_bayesmokken()
```

Note `shape = g` alongside `colour = g`. Every distinction in this package's
figures is carried by at least two channels, so nothing is lost in greyscale or
to a reader with colour-vision deficiency. When you extend a figure, keep that
property.

## Panels

```{r overview, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "A four-panel overview combining the scale coefficient, item coefficients, the bootstrap distribution and Monte Carlo stability into one figure."}
bm_plot_overview(fit)
```

With **patchwork** installed you can compose your own arrangements:

```{r patchwork, eval = has_patchwork, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Two package figures stacked vertically: item coefficients above, bootstrap distribution below."}
library(patchwork)
bm_plot_item_h(fit, sort = TRUE) / bm_plot_draws(fit)
```

## Saving for publication

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
p <- bm_plot_scale_h(fit)

# Vector, for a manuscript
ggsave("scale-h.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 4.4, device = cairo_pdf)

# Raster, when the venue insists
ggsave("scale-h.png", p, width = 7, height = 4.4, dpi = 600)
```

Prefer vector formats. The figures are line-and-point work, so they stay sharp
at any size and cost less than a raster at the same quality.

Keep the aspect ratio near the default. The dimensions were chosen so that item
labels stay horizontal and legible; compressing the width forces rotation.

## Accessibility

Two things travel with a figure, and only one of them is drawn.

**Redundant encoding.** Colour is never the only signal. Where a figure
distinguishes groups it also varies shape or linetype, and where it uses a
sequential scale it is one that survives conversion to greyscale.

**Alternative text.** Every figure in this package's documentation carries a
`fig.alt`, and a build check fails when one is missing. `bm_alt_text()`
proposes a starting point from the plot object:

```{r alt}
bm_alt_text(p_scale)
```

Treat it as a draft. Good alternative text states the exact displayed result
and the role of its guides, for example: “$H=0.130$, 95% CI [0.104, 0.162],
with descriptive reference guides at 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5.” It does not turn the
interval's location relative to a guide into a test or verdict.
